system_description.narrative_title: Fragmented order: tech shock, war, and shifting power competition
system_description.narrative_summary: The global order is an open, interdependent system in rapid reconfiguration: a US political shift (a Democratic 'blue wave') is immediately reshaping markets and policy, slowing an overheated AI/data‑centre buildout even as regional wars (Ukraine, Iran‑Gulf) keep energy and security risks elevated. Major‑power competition is intensifying — China is locking down critical‑minerals and economic levers while Russia and Iran press military and proxy options — all amid rising cyberattacks, crypto insecurity and financial stress. These interacting processes create feedback loops across markets, technology supply chains, and regional security architectures that drive systemic volatility.
system_description.scope: Nation-states and major powers (US, China, Russia, EU, Iran, etc.); financial markets (equities, bonds, crypto); technology and industrial ecosystems (AI, data centres, semiconductors); energy and commodity supply chains; cyber and information domains; regional conflicts (Ukraine, Middle East) and domestic political cycles that feed international policy.
system_description.super_system: The planetary socio-economic-technical system shaped by globalization, technological transformation (AI/digital infrastructure), and climate and resource constraints.
adjacent_subsystems: Global financial markets and credit system
International tech-industrial complex (AI, semiconductors, data centres)
Regional security architectures (Europe/NATO, Middle East security complex, Indo-Pacific balance)

variables.name: Russia–Ukraine war
variables.description: Russia and Ukraine remain locked in a sustained high‑intensity war whose battlefield dynamics and diplomatic manoeuvres are reshaping European security alignments.

variables.name: Iran‑Gulf regional escalation
variables.description: Iran, its regional proxies and Gulf states are engaged in an escalating campaign of strikes and maritime pressure—backed and countered by outside mediators—that is raising the risk of wider confrontation and perturbing global energy flows.

variables.name: Sino‑US geoeconomic rivalry
variables.description: China and the United States are contesting economic and technological primacy through trade, investment and influence strategies that are reordering supply chains, market access and global governance levers.

variables.name: AI infrastructure and market reallocation
variables.description: Major technology firms, investors and regulators are driving a rapid AI‑led industrial transition—marked by a surge (and subsequent correction) in data‑centre and semiconductor investment and growing regulatory scrutiny—that is reallocating economic and strategic power across sectors.

variables.name: Cyber attacks on critical systems
variables.description: State‑linked and criminal cyber actors are increasingly targeting critical infrastructure and financial platforms—disrupting logistics, food cold‑chains and exchanges—and prompting tighter defensive measures and regulatory attention.
